plain_english_title: What Changed on July 3, 1997 in VA Muscle-Injury Ratings—and Why Surgical Debridement Matters
what_this_means: Comparing the pre-July 3, 1997 and current versions of 38 C.F.R. § 4.56 highlights two practical details: first, in both eras, surgical debridement (removing damaged tissue from a deep wound) and prolonged infection appear in the Moderately Severe and Severe grades rather than the Moderate grade; second, certain muscle groups—such as the posterior thigh/hamstrings (Diagnostic Code 5313) and gluteal muscles (Diagnostic Code 5317)—carry higher percentage steps even at lower severity tiers, and upper-body injuries distinguish between the dominant and non-dominant arm.
record_clues: In-service hospital summaries describing 'debridement of wound track,' 'comminuted fracture with muscle damage,' or 'compartment syndrome / fasciotomy.'
Upper-arm, shoulder, or forearm shrapnel (SFW) or bullet injuries where right-handed vs. left-handed dominance was never noted on the rating sheet.
Posterior thigh (hamstring) or buttock/hip shrapnel wounds rated 0% as superficial scars despite documented muscle-group involvement.
important_cautions: VA's anti-pyramiding rules (38 C.F.R. §§ 4.14 and 4.55) restrict combining a muscle rating and a joint range-of-motion rating when both compensate the exact same movement limitation, though painful or disfiguring skin scars can often be rated separately.
Retained metallic fragments alone do not automatically establish a Severe rating; VA looks at the wound mechanism, tissue loss, and functional muscle symptoms recorded at the time.

Before challenging an older Board of Veterans' Appeals decision, discuss 38 C.F.R. § 20.1409(c)'s limit of one final merits CUE decision per prior Board decision on an issue with an accredited representative.
questions_for_representative: Which specific anatomical Muscle Group (I through XXIII, Diagnostic Codes 5301–5323) matches the entrance-to-exit path shown in my surgical or C&P exam records?
Did my in-service treatment involve surgical debridement or prolonged hospitalization, and how did the version of 38 C.F.R. § 4.56 in effect on my decision date classify that history?
For an upper-extremity wound, did VA apply the correct major (dominant) or minor (non-dominant) percentage column?
